title: Why Jairus Had to Watch Jesus Stop for Someone Else First
paragraphs: Why Jairus Had to Watch Jesus Stop for Someone Else First
The crowd would not stop pressing.

Dust climbed into the air beneath hundreds of feet. Bodies shoved shoulder against shoulder. Desperation breathed heavily through the streets that day because whenever Jesus walked into a city, suffering followed Him.
Demons screamed when He came near.
And somewhere inside that chaos was a father trying not to collapse.
Not a fisherman. Not a beggar. Not an outcast.
But pain has a way of stripping titles off people.
Because when your child is dying, reputation suddenly feels worthless.
In Greek, the name appears as Ἰάειρος (Iaeiros), derived from the Hebrew יָאִיר (Ya'ir), meaning “he enlightens” or “God gives light.”
But that day, everything around Jairus probably felt dark.
“Then came one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, and seeing Him, he fell at His feet.”
The Greek phrase used here is:
πίπτει πρὸς τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ (piptei pros tous podas autou)
Not bows politely. Not greets respectfully.
A man whose world was breaking in real time.
Old enough to laugh loudly. Old enough to recognize her father’s footsteps. Old enough to still reach for his hand when afraid.
And Jairus watches her slipping away.
You can almost hear the panic in his voice when he begs Jesus:
“My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay Your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live.” (Mark 5:23)
The Greek word Jairus uses for “little daughter” is:
It is intensely affectionate. A tender diminutive. Like saying: “My precious little girl.”
This was not theology to him.
Imagine Jairus feeling hope return for the first time in days.
The miracle worker is walking toward his house.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal for almost everyone who has followed God long enough.
Because many believers know exactly what it feels like to watch Jesus stop for someone else while your own prayer still feels unanswered.
But somehow heaven seems to pause for another person while your crisis keeps bleeding.
And if we are honest, this part of the story hurts.
Because Jairus had to stand there and watch Jesus give attention to someone whose suffering interrupted his own emergency.
“And a great crowd followed Him and thronged about Him.” (Mark 5:24)
Then suddenly, hidden inside that crowd, was a woman.
Mark 5:25 says she had suffered for twelve years.
The same amount of time Jairus had his daughter.
One father had twelve years of laughter with a child.
One woman had twelve years of isolation with pain.
One Savior walking between both of them.
The woman suffered from what Scripture calls a “flow of blood.”
According to Levitical law in Leviticus 15, her condition made her ceremonially unclean.
People avoided her. People feared contamination from her. People likely withdrew physical affection from her.
No normal touch. No normal relationships. No normal life.
Imagine surviving twelve years without being embraced.
Some people reading this understand that kind of loneliness more than they want to admit.
She spent everything trying to get healed.
“She had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better but rather grew worse.” (Mark 5:26)
The Greek phrase for “suffered much” is brutal:
That kind of suffering exhausts the soul.
Then she hears Jesus is near.
And suddenly faith rises inside her.
“For she said, ‘If I touch even His garments, I will be made well.’”
ἐὰν ἅψωμαι κἂν τῶν ἱματίων αὐτοῦ σωθήσομαι (ean hapsōmai kan tōn himatiōn autou sōthēsomai)
Literally: “If I may touch even His clothes, I shall be saved/healed.”
The word σωθήσομαι (sōthēsomai) comes from σώζω (sōzō).
It means: Saved. Rescued. Delivered. Made whole.
She was not merely seeking symptom relief.
No delay. No process. No gradual recovery.
And right there is where Jairus probably starts struggling internally.
And now Jesus turns around asking:
The crowd is crushing Him from every direction.
But Jesus is not talking about accidental contact.
He is talking about intentional faith.
Then the woman comes forward trembling.
Mark says she told Him “the whole truth.”
The shame. The pain. The loneliness. The failed treatments. The fear.
Meanwhile Jairus is watching the clock on his daughter’s life disappear.
“While He was still speaking, there came from the ruler’s house some who said, ‘Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?’”
And perhaps this is where many people secretly wrestle with God.
Because sometimes it feels like heaven delayed until the situation died.
And maybe what hurts even more is watching God move for other people while your own miracle seems buried.
But then Jesus says something powerful to Jairus.
μὴ φοβοῦ, μόνον πίστευε (mē phobou, monon pisteue)
Jesus was not merely commanding one moment of faith.
He was calling Jairus into continuing trust while everything looked irreversible.
Anyone can believe before the funeral.
Believing after the bad news arrives is different.
Death has already written its conclusion.
“The child is not dead but sleeping.”
The Greek word used implies mockery.
Because the world often mocks what Jesus is about to resurrect.
Then Jesus walks into the room.
Only Peter, James, John, and the parents remain.
And then one of the most beautiful moments in Scripture happens.
Mark preserves the original Aramaic words Jesus spoke.
Mark even translates it for us:
“Little girl, I say to you, arise.” (Mark 5:41)
But the depth of this moment is astonishing.
It could carry the warmth of saying: “Little lamb.” “Sweet child.”
The Creator of life stands over death itself and speaks gently.
No panic. No struggle. No uncertainty.
He was revealing something Jairus could not have understood earlier.
If Jesus had arrived before her death, Jairus would have only known Jesus as healer.
But because Jesus delayed, Jairus discovered Jesus as resurrection.
Some of the hardest delays in life are actually revealing dimensions of Christ we would never encounter otherwise.
Many people want God to hurry.
But sometimes Jesus permits the situation to cross human impossibility because resurrection glory looks different than ordinary intervention.
In John 11:6, after hearing Lazarus was sick, Jesus intentionally stayed two more days.
And when He finally arrived, Martha said:
“Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.”
That sentence still lives in many hearts today.
But Jesus operates with eternal vision while humans see only immediate pain.
“For My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways, declares the Lord.”
It refers to intentions, plans, purposes.
And that truth becomes painfully difficult when waiting collides with grief.
But the Gospel repeatedly shows something astonishing:
Jesus is never intimidated by what humans call impossible.
Dead daughters. Dead dreams. Dead hearts. Dead futures.
Nothing is beyond resurrection when Christ enters the room.
And perhaps someone reading this feels exactly like Jairus.
Then Jesus seemed to stop for somebody else.
Maybe you watched another person get the marriage restored. Another person get healed. Another person get blessed. Another person get the open door.
Meanwhile your own situation got worse.
And quietly, secretly, your heart started asking:
Jesus was still walking toward his house the entire time.
Even when heaven feels silent, Christ may still be moving toward you.
And there is another layer hidden inside this story that many miss.
The Gospel destroys human ranking systems.
Jesus stopped for the hidden woman while still caring for the influential father.
He is not limited by human urgency.
He can carry compassion for both at once.
And maybe that is part of what Jairus needed to learn.
Someone else’s breakthrough is not proof God abandoned you.
Another person’s healing is not evidence that heaven skipped your name.
Jesus stopping for her did not mean He stopped loving Jairus.
Because envy quietly poisons many believers.
People celebrate testimonies while others suffer silently behind screens.
But the Kingdom of God is not running out of mercy.
Jesus did not have to choose between the bleeding woman and Jairus’ daughter.
“And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good.”
Death is not good. Pain is not good. Grief is not good.
But God is able to work through even devastating moments toward eternal redemption.
The disciples thought everything was over.
Jesus was beaten. Mocked. Crucified. Buried.
For three days heaven looked silent.
Christianity is built on the reality that God brings life out of what humans bury.
That is why believers still have hope.
But because Christ defeated death itself.
The Greek word for resurrection is:
The Gospel is a resurrection story from beginning to end.
And maybe some people reading this need to hear something difficult but healing:
Jesus stopping for someone else first does not mean your story is over.
Sometimes heaven’s delay is preparing a deeper revelation of who Christ truly is.
The same Jesus who spoke “Talitha koum” over a dead child still speaks life today.
Not every earthly story ends the way people hope.
Scripture never promises a pain-free life.
But it does promise that those who belong to Christ are held by One stronger than death itself.
“O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?”
And because of Jesus, death is no longer the final sentence for those who trust Him.
Maybe this article found you at the exact moment your faith has been exhausted.
Maybe you have been smiling publicly while grieving privately.
Maybe you have watched Jesus bless others while your own heart quietly breaks.
Do not assume silence means abandonment.
Jairus probably thought the story was over too.
Until Jesus walked into the room.
And maybe that is the line your soul needed today.
Jesus still walks into impossible rooms.
This story hits differently when you have already experienced disappointment.
Sometimes Jesus lets the situation die because resurrection reveals His glory more deeply than rescue ever could.
Bakit Kailangang Panoorin ni Jairus si Jesus na Huminto Para sa Ibang Tao Muna
Makapal ang alikabok sa daan habang pilit sinusundan ng karamihan si Jesus. May mga umiiyak. May mga sumisigaw. May mga umaasang makahawak man lang sa Kanya kahit sandali.
At sa gitna ng lahat ng iyon, may isang ama na unti-unti nang nadudurog.
May pangalan. May respeto. May posisyon.
Pero may isang bagay na kayang durugin kahit ang pinakamataas na tao.
Kapag ang anak mo na ang mamamatay.
“God gives light.” “O ang Diyos ang nagbibigay ng liwanag.”
Pero sa araw na iyon, parang wala nang liwanag sa buhay niya.
“Dumating ang isa sa mga pinuno ng sinagoga, na ang pangalan ay Jairus; at pagkakita niya kay Jesus, siya ay nagpatirapa sa paanan nito.”
πίπτει πρὸς τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ (piptei pros tous podas autou)
Dahil minsan, ang sakit kayang iluhod kahit ang pinakamalakas.
Ang anak niyang babae ay mamamatay na.
At pansinin kung paano ito sinabi ni Jairus.
Maraming ama ang hindi umiiyak sa harap ng tao.
Pero sa araw na iyon, wala nang pride si Jairus.
Naglakad Siya papunta sa bahay nila.
Isipin mo ang pag-asa na bumalik kay Jairus.
At dito nagiging sobrang personal ang kwentong ito.
Dahil maraming Kristiyano ang nakaka-relate dito nang sobra.
Ikaw ang unang nagdasal. Ikaw ang desperado. Ikaw ang umiiyak gabi-gabi.
Pero parang ibang tao muna ang pinapansin ng Diyos.
At hindi natin kailangang magpanggap na hindi.
Habang naglalakad si Jesus kasama si Jairus, may isang babae sa gitna ng maraming tao.
Ang anak ni Jairus ay labindalawang taong gulang.
Labindalawang taon ding naghihirap ang babae.
Habang si Jairus ay may labindalawang taon ng masasayang alaala kasama ang anak niya…
Ang babaeng ito naman ay may labindalawang taon ng sakit.
Ayon sa Kautusan sa Levitico 15, marumi siyang itinuturing dahil sa kondisyon niya.
Marahil matagal na siyang hindi nayayakap.
Maraming taong buhay pero matagal nang walang nakakaramdam ng pagmamahal.
Baka may nagbabasa nito ngayon na ganoon din ang pakiramdam.
Humingi siya ng tulong sa maraming manggagamot.
Sakit ng pag-asang paulit-ulit na namamatay.
Pero nang marinig niyang dumadaan si Jesus, may nabuhay sa puso niya.
“Kahit mahawakan ko lang ang Kanyang damit, gagaling ako.”
ἐὰν ἅψωμαι κἂν τῶν ἱματίων αὐτοῦ σωθήσομαι (ean hapsōmai kan tōn himatiōn autou sōthēsomai)
Hindi lang katawan niya ang sugatan.
At dito siguro nagsimulang mabiyak ang puso ni Jairus.
Pero si Jesus nakikinig sa kwento ng ibang tao.
At minsan ganiyan din ang pakiramdam natin.
Habang nagsasalita pa si Jesus sa babae, may dumating.
Iyon na siguro ang pinakamasakit na pangungusap na narinig niya sa buong buhay niya.
At baka may nagbabasa nito ngayon na may sarili ring “patay na” sa puso.
At minsan ang pinakamahirap tanggapin ay ito:
Habang ikaw nasasaktan… parang may ibang pinagpapala ang Diyos.
Pero pagkatapos sabihin iyon kay Jairus, may sinabi si Jesus na sobrang lalim.
μὴ φοβοῦ, μόνον πίστευε (mē phobou, monon pisteue)
Literal: “Tigilan mong matakot. Magpatuloy kang maniwala.”
Madaling maniwala bago dumating ang masamang balita.
Pero paano kapag mukhang tapos na talaga?
Paano kapag parang wala nang pag-asa?
Pagdating nila sa bahay, umiiyak na ang lahat.
Final na para sa kanila ang lahat.
Tinatawanan nila ang mga bagay na bubuhayin ng Diyos.
Pagkatapos, pumasok si Jesus sa silid.
Kasama lang Niya sina Pedro, Santiago, Juan, at ang mga magulang.
At pagkatapos… sinabi Niya ang isa sa pinakamagandang linya sa buong Biblia.
Ang Maylikha ng buhay ay nagsalita lang.
At dito natin naiintindihan ang isang napakalalim na bagay.
Kung dumating si Jesus bago mamatay ang bata, makikilala lang sana Siya ni Jairus bilang manggagamot.
Pero dahil na-delay… nakilala niya si Jesus bilang muling pagkabuhay.
Minsan ang dahilan kung bakit hinahayaan ng Diyos na lumampas sa impossible ang sitwasyon… ay dahil may mas malalim Siyang gustong ipakita tungkol sa Kanyang sarili.
Siya ang Hari kahit sa ibabaw ng kamatayan.
Maraming tao ang galit sa delay ng Diyos.
Pero ang delay ay hindi laging rejection.
Minsan preparation ito para sa mas dakilang kapahayagan.
“Lord, kung nandito Ka sana, hindi sana namatay ang kapatid ko.”
Ang daming tao ang may ganyang dasal.
“Lord, kung gumalaw Ka lang sana agad…”
“Lord, kung sinagot Mo lang sana ako noon…”
Pero ang nakikita natin ay kasalukuyang sakit.
Ang nakikita ng Diyos ay eternal na layunin.
“For My thoughts are not your thoughts…”
May nakikita ang Diyos na hindi natin nakikita.
Pero paulit-ulit itong pinapakita ng Ebanghelyo:
Hindi natatakot si Jesus sa impossible.
Patay na pangarap. Patay na relasyon. Patay na puso. Patay na pananampalataya.
Kayang buhayin ng Diyos ang akala nating tapos na.
At baka may nagbabasa nito ngayon na parang si Jairus.
Pero parang iba muna ang pinagpapala.
Pero hindi iyon ang kwento ni Jairus.
Pero tuloy pa rin Siyang naglalakad papunta sa bahay nila.
Kahit tahimik ang langit… maaaring papunta pa rin si Jesus sa sitwasyon mo.
At may isa pang bagay dito na madalas hindi napapansin.
Pero pareho silang mahal ni Jesus.
Hindi porket pinagpala ang iba ay ibig sabihin nakalimutan ka na.
Hindi nauubusan ng awa ang Diyos.
Kayang hawakan ni Jesus ang sugat ng babae habang papunta pa rin Siya sa bahay ni Jairus.
At kaya rin Niyang hawakan ang sitwasyon mo ngayon.
Hindi ibig sabihin lahat ay mabuti.
Pero kayang gamitin ng Diyos kahit ang pinakamasakit na bagay para sa mas dakilang redemption.
Kahit ang krus mukhang pagkatalo noon.
Pero parating na pala ang resurrection.
Hindi na ang kamatayan ang huling salita.
At baka ito mismo ang kailangan mong marinig ngayon:
Hindi porket huminto si Jesus para sa ibang tao ay tapos na ang kwento mo.
Baka papunta pa lang Siya sa silid ng impossible sa buhay mo.
Mas malalim tamaan ng kwentong ito ang mga taong nasaktan na talaga.
Minsan hinahayaan ni Jesus na mamatay ang sitwasyon dahil ang resurrection ay magpapakita ng Kanyang kaluwalhatian nang mas malalim kaysa ordinaryong rescue.
